ABSTRACT: Efficient access to multiple functionalized allenes via a three component 1,4-alkylcyanation of enynes with cyclic
alcohol derivatives in the presence of trimethylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN) under copper/photoredox dual catalysis has been developed.
Both easily transformable aldehyde and cyano groups were introduced to tetra-substituted allenes through light-induced C−C bond
cleavage of cyclic butanol and pentanol derivatives. The reactions proceeded smoothly under mild conditions with broad functional
groups tolerance.
A
llenes represent an important class of molecules, which
are ubiquitous in natural products and pharmaceuticals as
well as functional materials.
1
In addition, they play crucial roles
in organic synthesis and drug design.
2
Thus, continuous efforts
were devoted to the assembly of functionalized allenes, and
several strategies such as sigmatropic rearrangement, β-
eliminations, and nucleophilic substitutions have been
successfully developed.
3
However, the aforementioned tradi-
tional methods mainly relied on prefunctionalization of starting
materials. Conjugated 1,3-enynes bearing multiple reactive
sites have been established as important synthons in organic
synthesis.
4
Recently, transition-metal-catalyzed radical-involv-
ing difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes has emerged as an
appealing and powerful tool for the construction of multi-
substituted allenes (Scheme 1a).
5
Although a number of
elegant synthetic methods have been reported by Ma,
6
Liu,
7
Bao,
8
Wu,
9
Li,
10
and other groups,
11
1,4-dicarbofunctionaliza-
tion of enynes to afford tetrasubstituted allenes has been less
explored.
12
For instance, in 2019, trasition-metal-catalyzed 1,4-
alkylarylation of enyes using boronic acids as nucleophiles was
reported by Wang
13
and Bao,
14
respectively, offering rapid
access to tetra-substituted aryl allenes. In 2022, Kong and co-
workers developed an efficient synthesis of multifunctionalized
CF
3
-allenes via nickel/photoredox catalysis.
15
Very recently, a
cross-electrophile 1,4-alkylarylation of 1,3-enynes using alkyl
and aryl bromides was reported by Deng, Chen, and co-
workers.
16

Strained ring derivatives such as cyclobutanone oxime esters
and substituted cyclopropanols have been well established as
precursors of functionalized primary radicals via C−C bond
cleavage.
17
In addition, alkylcyanation of unsaturated groups
afforded efficient approaches to functional molecules with
multiple C−C bond formations.
18
In 2021, the Ma group
reported a pioneering copper-catalyzed three component 1,4-
alkylcyanation of enynes using cyclobutanone oxime esters in
the presence of trimethylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN) or trimethyl-
(trifluoromethyl)silane (TMSCF
3
), providing facile access to
1,7-double-functionalized allenes (Scheme 1b).
6a
In the same
year, a novel N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-catalyzed radical
1,4-alkylcarbonylation of 1,3-enynes was developed by Du and
co-workers (Scheme 1c).
19a
However, these reports were
mostly limited to the construction of 1,7-double-functionalized
allenes. The development of novel 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization
methods of 1,3-enynes for synthesizing diverse multiple-
functionalized allenes is in continuous demand. Herein, we
have developed an efficient approach to access 1,7- and 1,8-
double-functionalized allenes via a three component 1,4-
alkylcyanation of enynes under copper/photoredox dual
catalysis (Scheme 1d). Both cyclic butanol and pentanol
derivatives were suitable in the reaction, serving as efficient
aldehyde-containing primary radical precursors via a C−C
bond cleavage.
20
By using this method, easily transformable
aldehyde and cyano groups were introduced to tetra-
substituted allenes under mild reaction conditions in the
presence of TMSCN.
The study was initiated with non-1-en-3-yn-2-ylbenzene
(1a), 2-cyclobutoxyisoindoline-1,3-dione (2a), and TMSCN as
model substrates using Ir(ppy)
3
as a photocatalyst with 20 W
blue LEDs as the light source under nitrogen atmosphere at
room temperature (Table 1). To our delight, when the
reaction was carried out with Cu(MeCN)
4
PF
6
as the cocatalyst
and 2,2′-bipyridine (L1) as the ligand in dichloromethane, the
desired product 3a was generated in 50% yield (entry 1).
Screening of solvents (entries 2−6) suggested that polar
solvents such as MeCN and DMF were more effective, and
product 3a was obtained in 93% and 98% yields, respectively.
The reaction was almost of equal efficiency when alkyl
substituted ligand L2 was used with DMF as the ideal choice of
solvent (entry 7). The reaction yield of 3a decreased to 43−
81% with L3−L5 as ligands (entries 8−10). Next, other copper
sources such as Cu(MeCN)
4

CuBr were tested, leading to a sharp decrease of the reaction
yield (entries 11−15). The reaction was totally suppressed
under the dark (entry 16).
With the optimized conditions in hand, we then moved our
attention to the substrate scope of 1,3-enynes (1) with 2-
cyclobutoxyisoindoline-1,3-dione (2a) as the reaction partner
in the presence of TMSCN (Scheme 2). Substitution of the
alkyne site (R
1
) was first investigated. Alkyl groups such as n-
pentyl, t-butyl, and i-butyl substituted products 3a−3c were
generated in moderate to excellent yields. Compound 3b was
obtained in lower yield, suggesting that the reactivity of the
allenyl radical was sensitive to steric hindrance under the
applied conditions. Cyclic alkyl groups including cyclopropyl
allenes 3d−3f were successfully achieved in excellent yields.
Functionalized aryl-substituted enynes participated in the
reaction smoothly, offering 3h−3k in moderate to good yields.
It is worthy to point out that aryl bromide remained stable
under the standard conditions. Satisfyingly, functional groups
such as Cl, Br, OAc, NHBoc, CN, and protected amines were
well tolerated, affording the corresponding products 3l−3s in
moderate to excellent yields. Next, the R
2
group of 1,3-enynes
was studied. Substrates bearing both electron-donating (OMe)
and -withdrawing (CN) groups of the phenyl ring proceeded
the reaction efficiently, delivering products 3u and 3v in 61%
and 72% yields, respectively. Naphthyl-, heteroaryl-, and alkyl-
substituted products 3w, 3x, and 3y were also given in good
yields. To further demonstrate the utility of this reaction, we
tested the three component allenation reaction with 1,3-enynes
derived from natural products (coumarin, L -phenylalanine,
glucose, and estrone) and drug molecules (flurbiprofen and
indometacin). The products 3z−3ae were uniformly obtained
in moderate to good yields.
Next, the scope of cyclic alcohol derivatives 2 was explored
(Scheme 3). Functional group substituted substrate 2b
participated in the reaction efficiently, offering access to the
corresponding products 4a and 4b in 52% and 67% yields,
respectively. Spirocyclic starting material 2c resulted in the
generation of 4c in 61% yield. Benzaldehyde substituted
product 4d was obtained in 73% yield from bicyclo[4.2.0]octa-
1,3,5-trien-7-ol derivative 2d. Satisfyingly, 1,8-double-function-
alized allenes 4e and 4f were successfully accessed, albeit in
moderate yields. However, when the reaction was carried out
with acyclic alcohol and cyclohexanol derivatives, no desired
products were generated under the standard conditions.
Gram-scale preparation of 3a was realized without a loss of
efficiency (Scheme 4A). Diverse transformations of the
product were realized, as exemplified in Scheme 4B. Alcohol
derivative 5a was generated via a reduction reaction with

nucleophilic addition of methylmagnesium bromide to the
aldehyde group generated 5c in 95% yield. Epoxidation of 3a

In order to gain further insight into the mechanism of this
novel transformation, some control experiments have been
conducted (Scheme 5). The allenation process was inhibited
when the reaction was run in the presence of 2.0 equiv of the

detected by HRMS analysis. Then, a radical clock experiment
using cyclopropyl 1,3-enyne 6 was carried out. Cyclopropyl-
substituted allene 7 instead of the ring-opening product was
isolated in 46% yield, indicating that the propargyl−allenyl
isomerization is faster than the ring-opening of the cyclopropyl

Based on the experimental results and literature reports,

a possible dual catalytic mechanism was depicted in Scheme 6.
The reaction was started by light-induced N−O bond cleavage,
generating oxygen radical A. Then, a β-scission formed the
aldehyde-functionalized primary radical B, which was trapped
by 1,3-enyne 1 to give intermediate C. The propargyl−allenyl
isomerization process furnished allenyl radical D, which was
captured by Cu
II
species to form allenyl-Cu
III
species E.
Subsequent reductive elimination generated the desired
product 3 and regenerated the Cu
I
species F. In the presence
of TMSCN, intermediate G was generated, which was oxidized
to Cu
II
via a single electron transfer process.
In conclusion, we have developed efficient access to multiple
functionalized allenes through a three component 1,4-
dicarbofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes. By combining light-
induced β-scission of cyclic butanol and pentanol derivatives
with copper catalyst, 1,7- and 1,8-double-functionalized allenes
were synthesized in the presence of TMSCN under mild
reaction conditions with broad functional group tolerance.
Late-stage modification of natural molecules and drugs was
realized by using this method.
